resources.string: Arabic letters
The 28 letters of the Arabic alphabet and how their shapes change within a word.
Short vowels
Fatḥa (a), kasra (i) and ḍamma (u): small marks above or below a letter.
Sukūn
A small mark on a letter, as in بۡ, meaning it has no vowel, so it closes the syllable.
Long vowels
Alif after fatḥa, wāw after ḍamma and yāʾ after kasra stretch the vowel to two counts (natural madd).
Tanwīn
A doubled vowel mark at the end of a word, read as the vowel followed by n: an, in, un.
Hamza
The catch in the throat (ء). It can stand alone or sit on an alif, wāw or yāʾ: أ إ ؤ ئ.
Tāʾ marbūṭa
The round tāʾ (ة) at the end of a word: read as t when continuing and as h when stopping.
Shadda
A mark that doubles a letter, as in بّ: the first one has a sukūn and the second one carries the vowel.
Dagger alif
A small alif written above a letter, as in مَٰ. It is read as a long ā.
Small wāw and yāʾ
A small wāw or yāʾ that shows a long vowel the spelling leaves out, as in بِهِۦ (bihī).
Hamzat al-waṣl
The alif with a small ṣād (ٱ). It is pronounced only when you start reading from this word, and silent when joined to the word before.
Silent letters
A small circle marks a letter that is written but never pronounced, like the final alif in كَفَرُواْ.
Stop signs
Small signs above the text, such as ج‎, صلى‎ and قلى‎, that tell you where stopping is allowed, better or required.
Prostration sign
The ۩ sign marks a place where the prostration of recitation (sajdat al-tilāwa) is made.
Heavy letters (tafkhīm)
Seven letters, خ ص ض غ ط ق ظ, are always pronounced with a full, heavy sound.
Lām shamsiyya (sun letters)
In ال before a sun letter, the lām is silent and the next letter is doubled: ٱلشَّمۡسِ (ash-shams).
Lām qamariyya (moon letters)
In ال before a moon letter, the lām is pronounced with a sukūn: ٱلۡقَمَرِ (al-qamar).
The lām in the name Allāh
The lām of ٱللَّه is heavy after a or u, and light after i, as in بِسۡمِ ٱللَّهِ.
Ghunnah
A nasal sound held for two counts on a noon or meem with shadda (نّ مّ).
Qalqalah
The letters ق ط ب ج د make a slight bounce when they have a sukūn or when you stop on them.
Noon sākinah and tanwīn
A noon without a vowel, and the n sound of tanwīn, is pronounced in one of four ways depending on the next letter. Idghām comes in two kinds: with and without ghunnah.
Iẓhār (clear)
Before a throat letter (ء ه ع ح غ خ) the noon is pronounced clearly, with no extra nasal sound.
Idghām with ghunnah
Before ي ن م و the noon merges into the next letter with a nasal sound.
Idghām without ghunnah
Before ل or ر the noon merges completely into the next letter, with no nasal sound.
Iqlāb
Before ب the noon turns into a hidden meem, shown by a small meem above it: نۢ.
Ikhfāʾ (hiding)
Before the other 15 letters the noon is hidden: between clear and merged, with a nasal sound.
Meem sākinah
A meem without a vowel is pronounced in one of three ways depending on the next letter.
Iẓhār shafawī
Before any letter except ب and م, the meem is pronounced clearly.
Idghām shafawī
A meem followed by another meem: the two merge into one doubled meem with a nasal sound.
Ikhfāʾ shafawī
Before ب the meem is hidden, with the lips lightly closed and a nasal sound.
Madd sign
The wavy line over a long vowel, as in آ, means: stretch it longer than the natural two counts.
Madd muttaṣil (connected)
A long vowel followed by a hamza in the same word is stretched 4 to 5 counts.
Madd munfaṣil (separated)
A long vowel at the end of a word, with a hamza at the start of the next word, is usually stretched 4 to 5 counts.
Madd lāzim (necessary)
A long vowel followed by a shadda or a fixed sukūn is always stretched 6 counts.
